newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- AUG 8.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- AUG 8.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

-- The government is trying to get a message across to the country's employers and labourforce that the 1998 Budget will be tight, too, because there is concern over the means by which revenue growth will accelerate without imposing new taxes. But tax brackets will be indexed, for the first time since 1992.
-- The finance ministry favours a shift to drachma borrowing by public utilities and corporations which are faced with a higher servicing cost on their debt in dollar and yen.

-- Effective September 1, 1997 there will be no differential treatment of foreign currency loans over drachma loans in Greece. Legislation was passed for a cut to 3.0 from 4.0 percent in the Special Tax on Banking Operations (EFTE) on interest payments and the uniform imposition of the 1.2 percent levy on interest rates of loans taken out in any currency.

-- The government will align its legislation to the European Union's over the award procedures of state contracts for supplies and public works. It seeks to protect its members from legal battles in Greek and European courts over partiality allegations and circumvent disturbing delays in infrastructure works and public investments.

-- Greece's seven largest state-run pension funds are in need of 400 billion drachmas in 1997, the second year in which their financial stance has deteriorated dramatically. The government is expected to take action following the completion of its 'social dialogue' with Greek employers and labour force.
-- The dollar eased from recent peaks in international markets as there are growing indications that central banks in major countries started to look into methods to reverse its rising trend.
-- Greek industrialists are prepared to rebuff recent attacks by the media over their alleged low contribution to the state's total fiscal revenues.
-- Legislation has been passed allowing individuals and company representatives sentenced for issuing cheques which bounced to monetise their penalties.

-- The government exerts pressure on European Union authorities to amend the terms of the so-called 'Santer' financial aid package, providing greater flexibility in the transfer of subsidies between different fiscal years and the approval of works qualifying for funding.

-- The new development law to be submitted to parliament in the autumn will be aimed at the increase in employment through a boom in investments, recognising that the ongoing stabilisation policy has little to offer to ease unemployment.

-- Petroleum companies operating in Greece attacked the government for the imposition of price limits on petrol prices, describing the measure as being 'anachronistic' and a form of 'indirect taxation'. --Angelos Kiosklis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
